entries.title: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
entries.claim: Users often perceive aesthetically pleasing design as design that’s more usable.

entries.title: Choice Overload
entries.claim: The tendency for people to get overwhelmed when they are presented with a large number of options, often used interchangeably with the term paradox of choice.

entries.title: Chunking
entries.claim: A process by which individual pieces of an information set are broken down and then grouped together in a meaningful whole.

entries.title: Cognitive Bias
entries.claim: A systematic error of thinking or rationality in judgment that influence our perception of the world and our decision-making ability.

entries.title: Cognitive Load
entries.claim: The amount of mental resources needed to understand and interact with an interface.

entries.title: Doherty Threshold
entries.claim: Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (<400ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other.

entries.title: Fitts’s Law
entries.claim: The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target.

entries.title: Flow
entries.claim: The mental state in which a person performing some activity is fully immersed in a feeling of energized focus, full involvement, and enjoyment in the process of the activity.

entries.title: Goal-Gradient Effect
entries.claim: The tendency to approach a goal increases with proximity to the goal.

entries.title: Hick’s Law
entries.claim: The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices.

entries.title: Jakob’s Law
entries.claim: Users spend most of their time on other sites. This means that users prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.

entries.title: Law of Common Region
entries.claim: Elements tend to be perceived into groups if they are sharing an area with a clearly defined boundary.

entries.title: Law of Proximity
entries.claim: Objects that are near, or proximate to each other, tend to be grouped together.

entries.title: Law of Prägnanz
entries.claim: People will perceive and interpret ambiguous or complex images as the simplest form possible, because it is the interpretation that requires the least cognitive effort of us.

entries.title: Law of Similarity
entries.claim: The human eye tends to perceive similar elements as a complete picture, shape, or group, even if those elements are separated.

entries.title: Law of Uniform Connectedness
entries.claim: Elements that are visually connected are perceived as more related than elements with no connection.

entries.title: Mental Model
entries.claim: A compressed model based on what we think we know about a system and how it works.

entries.title: Miller’s Law
entries.claim: The average person can only keep 7 (plus or minus 2) items in their working memory.

entries.title: Occam’s Razor
entries.claim: Among competing hypotheses that predict equally well, the one with the fewest assumptions should be selected.

entries.title: Paradox of the Active User
entries.claim: Users never read manuals but start using the software immediately.

entries.title: Pareto Principle
entries.claim: The Pareto principle states that, for many events, roughly 80% of the effects come from 20% of the causes.

entries.title: Parkinson’s Law
entries.claim: Any task will inflate until all of the available time is spent.

entries.title: Peak-End Rule
entries.claim: People judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak and at its end, rather than the total sum or average of every moment of the experience.

entries.title: Postel’s Law
entries.claim: Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send.

entries.title: Selective Attention
entries.claim: The process of focusing our attention only to a subset of stimuli in an environment — usually those related to our goals.

entries.title: Serial Position Effect
entries.claim: Users have a propensity to best remember the first and last items in a series.

entries.title: Tesler’s Law
entries.claim: Tesler's Law, also known as The Law of Conservation of Complexity, states that for any system there is a certain amount of complexity which cannot be reduced.

entries.title: Von Restorff Effect
entries.claim: The Von Restorff effect, also known as The Isolation Effect, predicts that when multiple similar objects are present, the one that differs from the rest is most likely to be remembered.

entries.title: Working Memory
entries.claim: A cognitive system that temporarily holds and manipulates information needed to complete tasks.

entries.title: Zeigarnik Effect
entries.claim: People remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed tasks. - Oval 9 Copy - Combined Shape - Rectangle 15
